newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RBA says profit from issuing notes fell in 1990s.
newsitem.headline: RBA says profit from issuing notes fell in 1990s.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) said the average annual profit made from the issue of notes and coins in Australia, known as seigniorage, has almost halved in this decade compared to the 1980s.

In a study paper on "Measuring Profits from Currency Issue" in its July Bulletin, the central bank said seigniorage since December 1991 had averaged 0.2 percent of gross domestic product against 0.4 percent in the prior decade. Even this reduced profit amounted to around A$1.0 billion a year, however.
The RBA also said notes and coins outstanding rose markedly in the first half of the 1990s to its highest level in 20 years.

The RBA explained that when a commercial bank requires additional notes to meet customer demand it buys them from the RBA in return for another financial asset the value of which is equal to the face value of the notes.
Seigniorage arises because the cost of producing the notes is much smaller than the value of the asset received by the RBA, the central bank said.
There were two ways of measuring seigniorage, one called the accrual method used by the RBA and a cash-flow method favoured by the Treasury, which issues all the coins used in Australia.
The RBA said that over recent years seiniorage from note issue using the accrual method had averaged 0.3 percent of GDP and 0.2 percent by the cash-flow approach.
"As a share of GDP, seiniorage is considerably below the levels earned in the 1980s when inflation and nominal interest rates were much higher," the bank said.

The bank noted that by international standards total seiniorage in Australia was neither particularly high nor low and cited examples of Germany where it averaged 0.5 percent of GDP over the period from 1992 to 1996 and the U.K. where it amounted to 0.17 percent.

The bank said the sharp rise in the value of notes and coins outstanding since the end of the 1980s -- from about 3.8 percent of GDP to more than 4.3 percent -- may have been partly caused by regulatory and taxation factors.

New laws such as the requirement on financial intermediaries to report large transactions, requirements for more stringent identification of depositors and the deeming of interest for the means test of pensions, may have encouraged some people to hold more of their wealth as cash, the bank said.
The importance of cash as a store of wealth was shown by the high proportion of A$100 noted in circulation.

Such notes accounted for almost 40 percent of the value of currency in Australia but since they were used infrequently for daily transactions, it followed that many were used for other purposes, the RBA said.
"For example, as a store of wealth or for transactions in the cash or underground economy," it said.
The premise was supported, the bank said, by the fact that on average a A$100 note returned to the RBA once a year while a A$20 note visited the bank five times.
